drills.q: A nightly load scheduled at 02:00 assumes an upstream extract always finishes by then. One night the extract runs 40 minutes late. What happens, and why is there no error?
drills.a: The 02:00 job runs anyway, on whatever partial data exists at that moment, producing a plausible but incomplete result. There's no error because cron has no mechanism to verify readiness — it only knows the clock, not the state of the upstream job.

drills.q: Someone proposes fixing the above by moving the schedule from 02:00 to 04:00. Why doesn't this actually solve the problem?
drills.a: It just moves the threshold at which the same failure recurs (what happens the night upstream is 3 hours late instead of 40 minutes) while costing 2 extra hours of latency every single night to hedge against a rare event. The structural fix is triggering on the upstream's actual completion signal, not a bigger guess.

drills.q: An event-driven pipeline (S3 event -> Lambda) has produced zero output for 6 hours with no errors logged anywhere, while partners confirm they've been uploading files normally. What class of failure is this, and what are your first two diagnostic steps?
drills.a: A silently broken event trigger — the classic failure mode of push-based triggering, which produces absence rather than an error. First: confirm files are actually landing in the expected bucket/prefix via S3 access logs. Second: check the event notification/EventBridge rule configuration for drift (IAM permission change, pattern that no longer matches, or a notification config silently overwritten).

drills.q: What single piece of monitoring would have caught the silently-broken trigger in the previous scenario sooner, and why does it work even though the trigger's own health checks wouldn't?
drills.a: An independent freshness/liveness check on the downstream table, alerting on staleness. It works because it monitors the outcome (is data landing) rather than the trigger mechanism's own reported health — since the trigger's failure mode is silence, its own signals go quiet right along with it and can't be relied on to detect the break.

drills.q: A team routes a high-volume (10,000 invocations/hour), short-lived, non-audit-critical image-resize workflow through Step Functions Standard and gets an unexpectedly large AWS bill. What's the fix and why?
drills.a: Move it to Express workflows. Standard is priced per state transition and gets expensive fast at high volume; Express is built for exactly this case (short-lived, high-throughput, non-audit-critical) at a fraction of the cost, trading away Standard's exactly-once guarantee and full execution history, which this workload doesn't need.

drills.q: A team migrates a workflow from Step Functions Standard to Express to cut costs, without changing any of the step logic. What new risk did they just introduce, and why?
drills.a: Express is at-least-once execution, unlike Standard's exactly-once guarantee, so a step can now be invoked more than once for the same logical event. If the step logic isn't idempotent, this can produce duplicate side effects (double-writes, double-charges) that Standard's guarantee had previously been absorbing silently.

drills.q: An SQS consumer's processing time for a batch of messages occasionally spikes well above the configured visibility timeout under load. What goes wrong, and what's the fix that doesn't require guessing a single fixed timeout that covers both fast and slow cases?
drills.a: A second consumer picks up the same message before the first one finishes, causing duplicate processing. Fix: a heartbeat/extend-visibility pattern where the consumer periodically calls ChangeMessageVisibility while work is genuinely still in progress, rather than trying to pick one static timeout that must cover both typical and worst-case durations.

drills.q: 200 partner files land in S3 at unpredictable times throughout the day, all needing the same transform, which calls a downstream API with a hard rate limit. Design the triggering and backpressure, and explain why a direct S3-event-to-Lambda-per-file design would fail.
drills.a: S3/EventBridge pushes an event to SQS on file arrival, decoupling arrival rate from processing rate; a consumer pulls from SQS at a pace that respects the API's rate limit, and bursts naturally queue instead of triggering many simultaneous rate-limit violations. A direct S3-event-to-Lambda-per-file design has no buffering layer — 50 files landing in one minute would fire 50 concurrent Lambda invocations all hitting the rate-limited API at once, with no backpressure mechanism to slow them down.

drills.q: When is it a legitimate, senior engineering choice to keep a pipeline on plain cron rather than migrating it to event-driven triggering, given everything wrong with cron's readiness assumption?
drills.a: When the upstream's completion time has a genuinely tight, well-understood, rarely-violated bound with its own actively monitored SLA — the risk is managed at the source rather than assumed silently. In that case the added infrastructure (event bus, rules, its own failure-mode monitoring) buys protection against a risk that's already independently controlled, making cron's simplicity the better tradeoff.

drills.q: Why would you choose EventBridge over native S3 Event Notifications for a pipeline that needs to reprocess the last 30 days of uploaded files after fixing a bug in the consumer?
drills.a: EventBridge supports archive-and-replay of events, letting you reprocess historical events without manually re-listing and re-invoking for every file. Native S3 Event Notifications have no such replay capability — you'd have to reconstruct the list of affected files yourself and manually re-trigger processing for each.
